details:
**Battle Royal**
In the first chapter, the narrator and other Black teenagers are forced to watch a "magnificent blonde" with an American flag tattooed on her stomach dance. They are then blindfolded and made to box each other for the entertainment of the town's white leaders. Afterward the boys scramble for coins on an electrified rug. The narrator then gives his graduation speech and slips by saying "social equality" instead of "social responsibility." He is rewarded with a briefcase and a scholarship to a Black college.

**Ras the Exhorter (Ras the Destroyer)**
Ras is a West Indian Black nationalist street speaker in Harlem who attacks the Brotherhood for working with white people. Near the end he becomes "Ras the Destroyer," riding a horse with a spear and shield during a Harlem race riot. The narrator throws Ras's own spear at him and it goes through his jaw.

**Dr. Bledsoe**
Bledsoe is the president of the narrator's college and appears to bow to white people while holding power for himself. He expels the narrator after the Mr. Norton disaster. He sends him to New York with sealed "letters of recommendation" that secretly tell employers to keep the boy "running." The narrator later dreams of a document that says the same thing.

**Mr. Norton and the Golden Day**
Norton is a rich white trustee of the college who sees the narrator as his "fate." While driving him, the narrator takes Norton to Jim Trueblood's cabin. When Norton faints, the narrator brings him to the Golden Day, a run-down bar and brothel full of mentally ill Black veterans. Norton is hurt there during a fight.

**Jim Trueblood**
Trueblood is a Black sharecropper who got his own daughter, Matty Lou, pregnant; his wife Kate was pregnant at the same time. He tells Norton about a dream in which a naked white woman tries to keep him "out of the clock," which he had just before sleeping with his daughter. Showing Norton this man is the main reason the narrator is expelled.

**The Brotherhood and Brother Jack**
The Brotherhood is a communist-style political group in Harlem led by Brother Jack. Jack recruits the narrator as a speaker. At his first rally the narrator speaks about the "dispossessed," and members criticize the speech for not being "scientific." In one meeting, Jack's glass eye falls into a glass of water, which shows he cannot really see clearly. The narrator later dreams that Jack castrates him.

**Liberty Paints and Lucius Brockway**
The narrator gets a factory job at Liberty Paints. Its famous "Optic White" paint is made by mixing in ten drops of black liquid, a symbol of race in America. In the boiler room he works for Lucius Brockway, an old Black worker who loses his dentures in a fight because he thinks the narrator is a union man after his job. Brockway sets off a boiler explosion that injures the narrator.

**Electroshock therapy at the factory hospital**
After the explosion, doctors give the narrator electroshock treatment inside a machine, a scene often read as a kind of rebirth. When they show him a card asking "What is your name?", he cannot remember his own name or his mother's. He thinks of folk characters like Buckeye the Rabbit (Brer Rabbit).

**1,369 light bulbs and Monopolated Light and Power**
In the prologue, the narrator lives hidden in a forgotten cellar of a whites-only building. He has wired 1,369 light bulbs and powers them with electricity stolen from Monopolated Light and Power. He ends up there after falling into an open manhole while running from men who want to know what is in his briefcase.

**Tod Clifton and the Sambo dolls**
Tod Clifton is a handsome young Brotherhood leader in Harlem who leaves the group, "plunging outside history." The narrator finds him on the street selling dancing paper Sambo dolls, a racist caricature. A police officer shoots Clifton dead. The narrator's speech at his funeral leads to his break with the Brotherhood.

**Rinehart**
Rinehart is never seen in the novel. He is a gambler, numbers runner, pimp, and reverend all at once. When the narrator puts on dark glasses and a wide hat, people keep mistaking him for Rinehart. This shows him how easily identity can change.

**Sybil**
Sybil is the drunk white wife of a Brotherhood member. The narrator seduces her to get information, choosing her over Jack's mistress Emma. Sybil fantasizes about being raped by a Black man. The narrator writes "Sybil, you were raped by Santa Claus. Surprise" on her stomach in lipstick.

**Mary Rambo**
Mary is a kind older Black woman in Harlem who takes in the narrator after the paint factory injury. She lets him stay without paying rent. He later lies to her about where he got the money to pay her back.

**Opening and closing lines**
The prologue opens: "I am an invisible man," and he says he is not a spook or a "Hollywood-movie ectoplasm." He is "of flesh and bone, fiber and liquids—and I might even be said to possess a mind." He is invisible "simply because people refuse to see me." The novel ends: "Who knows but that, on the lower frequencies, I speak for you?"

**Louis Armstrong's "(What Did I Do to Be So) Black and Blue"**
In the prologue, the narrator smokes marijuana and listens to this Armstrong recording, and his sense of time shifts. He sinks into imagined levels of the past and talks with an old slave woman who both loved and poisoned her master. He says he wants five record players all playing the song at once.
